meta.title: Texas Instruments (TXN): Haviv Ilan's 300mm Manufacturing Wager — How the World's Largest Analog Chipmaker Is Betting Internal Fabrication, a $60 Billion Capex Cycle, and the Silicon Labs Acquisition to Extend Its Industrial and Automotive Franchise Through the 2030s
meta.abstract:
Texas Instruments Incorporated is the world's largest analog semiconductor company by revenue, a position it has defended for more than two decades through catalog scale, long product life cycles, and a deliberate pivot toward internally owned 300-millimeter wafer manufacturing that no other pure-play analog competitor has matched at comparable volume. Under chairman, president, and chief executive Haviv Ilan—who assumed the CEO role in May 2023 and added the chairmanship in January 2026 following the retirement of 45-year company veteran Rich Templeton—TI has staked its long-run competitive advantage on a capital-allocation thesis as bold as anything in the semiconductor industry: sustain elevated capex through a multi-year inventory correction to build the lowest-cost analog capacity in the world, then harvest the resulting free-cash-flow inflection as demand recovers and depreciation cycles through.

The evidence that the thesis is beginning to deliver surfaced in the 2025 fiscal year and accelerated into early 2026. Fiscal 2025 revenue reached $17.68 billion, a 13% year-over-year recovery led by the Analog segment at $14.01 billion and Embedded Processing at $2.70 billion. SM1—TI's first 300mm fab in Sherman, Texas—began production in late 2025 after a three-and-a-half-year construction timeline. Free cash flow nearly doubled to $2.94 billion from $1.50 billion in 2024 as capital expenditures stepped down to $4.55 billion from $4.82 billion. Q1 2026 extended the trajectory: revenue of $4.83 billion grew 19% year-over-year, industrial expanded more than 30%, and data-center power management revenue grew approximately 90%, providing the first clear evidence of TI's relevance to the AI infrastructure buildout. Management guided Q2 2026 to $5.0–$5.4 billion, clearing Street consensus by more than 7%.

The strategic picture was materially enlarged on February 4, 2026, when TI announced the $7.5 billion all-cash acquisition of Silicon Labs—the market leader in wireless IoT connectivity ICs—at $231 per share. The transaction, which targets $450 million in annual synergies and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, will layer a comprehensive Bluetooth, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Sub-GHz, and Wi-Fi portfolio onto TI's analog and embedded-processing base, deepening the catalog and channel reach that are the company's primary customer-retention levers. It also introduces balance-sheet leverage and integration execution risk at a pivotal moment in the capex normalization arc, with long-term debt at $13.55 billion before the acquisition financing.

This dossier examines TI across five interlocking strategic threads: its 96-year corporate history from geophysical-services company to integrated circuit inventor to analog scale leader; the competitive moat embedded in 300mm internal manufacturing, a 100,000-plus part catalog, and 100,000-plus customer relationships; the free-cash-flow inflection thesis and its sensitivity to capex normalization, end-market cycle timing, and Silicon Labs integration execution; valuation benchmarked against ADI, Microchip, Infineon, STMicro, and NXP with explicit bull, base, and bear price scenarios; and the 12-month tactical and 2026–2030 strategic outlook under Ilan's capital-return-first framework.

chapters.title: The 300mm Bet: Texas Instruments at the Inflection Point, 2026
chapters.body:
## Manufacturing as Moat

Texas Instruments entered 2026 doing something its analog peers could not replicate: converting a multi-year, $60 billion-plus capital expenditure super-cycle into a structural manufacturing-cost advantage anchored in 300mm wafer fabrication that no pure-play competitor—not Analog Devices, not STMicroelectronics, not Microchip Technology—could match at comparable scale. The thesis, long articulated by management in investor presentations and dismissed by skeptics as capex overreach, arrived at its first empirical test in April 2026, when the company reported first-quarter revenue of $4.83 billion, a 19% year-over-year increase that beat the top of prior guidance by ~~roughly $150 million~~ ==roughly $145 million== and arrived alongside guidance for Q2 2026 of $5.0 billion to $5.4 billion. For a company whose stock had spent the prior two years absorbing the heaviest underutilization charges in its modern history, those numbers carried structural weight.

## The Inflection Confirmed

The Q1 2026 results were not simply a cyclical bounce. Industrial revenue—~~TI's largest and most important end market, representing roughly 40 to 45 percent of the business~~ ==TI's largest end market alongside Automotive, with each representing about 33 percent of revenue==—grew more than 30% year-over-year, confirming that the 2023–2024 inventory destocking cycle had cleared and that underlying demand in factory automation, grid infrastructure, and building systems was accelerating. Data-center power management, an emerging growth vector driven by hyperscaler demand for 48V power architecture ICs supporting AI accelerator infrastructure, expanded approximately 90% year-over-year. Net income reached $1.55 billion and diluted EPS $1.68.

Against that backdrop, the full-year 2025 figures told a more important story about trajectory. Free cash flow nearly doubled—to $2.94 billion, or 16.6% of revenue—from $1.50 billion the prior year, as capital expenditures declined modestly to $4.55 billion from $4.82 billion and operating cash flow reached $7.15 billion. ~~That FCF/revenue ratio of 16.6% remains well below management's stated long-run target of 25 to 35%~~ ==By the May 2026 snapshot, trailing-12-month free cash flow had climbed further to roughly $4.35 billion, lifting the FCF/revenue ratio toward about 23 percent and into reach of the lower bound of management's stated long-run target of 25 to 35 percent==, but its direction of travel—nearly doubling in a single fiscal year—validated the thesis that the company was past the trough of the investment cycle's earnings drag.

| Metric | FY2024 | FY2025 | YoY Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $15.64B | $17.68B | +13% |
| Operating income | ~~$4.5B~~ ==$5.47B== | $6.02B | ~~+34%~~ ==+10%== |
| Operating margin | ~~29%~~ ==34.9%== | 34.1% | ~~+510 bps~~ ==-80 bps== |
| Free cash flow | $1.50B | $2.94B | +96% |
| FCF / Revenue | 9.6% | 16.6% | +700 bps |
| Capex | $4.82B | $4.55B | -6% |

## Haviv Ilan's Wager

At the center of this manufacturing conviction stood Haviv Ilan—Israeli-born, an electrical engineer who joined Texas Instruments in 1999 through the company's acquisition of Butterfly Communications and rose through successive roles in wireless connectivity and fab operations before becoming chief operating officer in 2020 and chief executive in May 2023. In January 2026, he assumed the chairmanship as well, consolidating governance and operational authority in a single executive at precisely the moment the strategy's validation window opened. Ilan had inherited a capex commitment of historic magnitude and a stock trading near cycle lows; by May 2026, TXN had re-rated nearly 80% from its 2024 trough to approach $325, a move that priced in both the FCF inflection and, perhaps, a degree of optimism about the thesis's durability that left little room for execution error.

## The Silicon Labs Variable

Into that already-complex trajectory, TI inserted a strategic bet of a different kind. On February 4, 2026, the company announced a definitive agreement to acquire Silicon Laboratories for $231.00 per share in cash—a total enterprise value of approximately $7.5 billion—in a transaction that would make Texas Instruments the second-largest wireless IoT connectivity IC company globally, with combined presence in Bluetooth, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Sub-GHz, Thread, and Wi-Fi. The industrial logic was coherent: TI's factory-automation and smart-building customers increasingly needed wireless-connected sensor nodes, and offering that wireless capability within the TI catalog reduced system architects' vendor count. The financial logic was more demanding. The deal, expected to close in the first half of 2027 pending regulatory clearances, would be funded through cash on hand and investment-grade debt issuance, pushing gross debt from $13.55 billion toward an estimated $19 to $21 billion at close and compressing interest coverage ratios from roughly 7 to 8 times toward 4 to 6 times.

> "Our focus is on free cash flow per share growth over the long term."

That phrase, repeated by Ilan and his predecessors across years of earnings calls, carried particular weight in 2026. Silicon Labs arrived not as a distraction from the manufacturing thesis but as a potential extension of it: the $450 million in annual synergies management targeted within three years of close depended substantially on migrating Silicon Labs' outsourced 8-inch foundry volumes onto TI's own 300mm fabs—a 2 to 4 year migration process that would only begin after the deal closed in 2027.

## Three Questions This Dossier Will Answer

The chapters that follow examine Texas Instruments as a company at a genuine strategic inflection, not merely a cyclical recovery. Three questions will frame the inquiry. First: can TI's 300mm capacity load fast enough—given SM1 beginning production at Sherman in late 2025 and LFAB2 approaching first output in 2026—to sustain free cash flow growth while simultaneously absorbing the Silicon Labs acquisition debt? Second: does the electrification of industrial systems and automotive platforms provide a demand runway long enough, and deep enough in analog content per unit, to justify a decade-long investment cycle that will not yield peak economics until the early 2030s? Third: at a market capitalization of approximately $290 billion—roughly three times Analog Devices, six times Microchip, and carrying forward price-to-earnings of approximately 38 times—is TXN priced for a durable structural moat, or for a manufacturing thesis that still requires years of execution to validate?

The answers will determine whether Haviv Ilan's wager, made in silicon and steel across Sherman, Texas and Lehi, Utah, stands as the defining industrial capital-allocation decision of the 2020s.

chapters.title: From Geophysical Service Incorporated to Integrated Circuit Inventor to Analog Scale Leader, 1930–2026
chapters.body:
## From Seismic Surveys to Silicon: The GSI Origins, 1930–1951

The company that would one day design the world's most widely distributed analog chips began not in a laboratory but in an oil field. In 1930, geophysicist John Clarence Karcher and petroleum geologist Eugene McDermott co-founded Geophysical Service Incorporated in Newark, New Jersey, to commercialize seismic reflection technology for locating subsurface oil deposits. GSI relocated to Dallas in 1934, drawn by proximity to the Texas petroleum industry. The business was entrepreneurial and technically demanding — seismic crews deployed sensitive instruments across desolate terrain, and the science required continuous refinement of electronics for signal acquisition and processing. That applied-electronics capability would prove decisive.

World War II transformed GSI from an oil-services company into a defense electronics manufacturer. The Navy needed equipment to detect submarines, and GSI's instrument engineers were among the few with the requisite skills. Defense contracts flowed in; the business expanded rapidly. By the late 1940s, the scientific instrument division had grown large enough to stand as a separate enterprise. In 1951, a group led by Erik Jonsson, Cecil Green, Eugene McDermott, and Henry Bates Peacock completed a corporate reorganization, incorporating the instrument business as General Instruments Inc. — a name almost immediately changed to Texas Instruments Incorporated to avoid confusion with an existing New York electronics firm.

The renamed company moved quickly into semiconductors. In 1952, TI licensed transistor technology from Bell Laboratories, then the most valuable technology license available, and began manufacturing germanium transistors commercially. Two years later, TI engineer Gordon Teal achieved a process breakthrough in growing large single-crystal silicon rods, enabling TI to introduce the world's first commercial silicon transistor in 1954 — a material advance that gave the company a critical manufacturing edge over competitors still reliant on the less reliable germanium.

## The Kilby Moment, September 12, 1958

No event in Texas Instruments' history carries more structural weight than what happened in a Dallas laboratory on a Tuesday morning in early autumn 1958. Jack St. Clair Kilby had joined TI only months earlier, in May. As a new employee, he lacked the seniority to take vacation during the company's summer shutdown, so he remained in the lab while colleagues departed. The isolation proved generative. Working with a small sliver of germanium roughly the size of a pencil tip, Kilby built a circuit — a phase-shift oscillator — in which all components, including transistors, resistors, and capacitors, were fabricated from a single continuous piece of semiconductor material, connected not by wires soldered to separate components but by fine gold bonds across the surface of the germanium itself. On September 12, with colleagues watching, he connected the device to an oscilloscope and applied power. A continuous sine wave appeared on the screen.

Kilby filed a patent on February 6, 1959, titled "Miniaturized Electronic Circuits." The application would become one of the most contested in technological history. At Fairchild Semiconductor in Mountain View, California, Robert Noyce had been developing a conceptually similar but technically distinct approach — a planar integrated circuit that used photolithographic patterning and evaporated aluminum interconnects rather than Kilby's wire bonds. Fairchild's planar process was, in many respects, more manufacturable. The ensuing patent dispute between TI and Fairchild dragged through courts and cross-licensing negotiations for more than a decade before the two companies reached a broad settlement in 1966. The legal resolution was essentially commercial: both companies shared the market rather than one crushing the other. The cultural residue was competitive — and it established process intellectual property as the central weapon in the semiconductor industry's long history of rivalry.

Kilby's invention received its ultimate recognition in October 2000, when the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded him the Nobel Prize in Physics. The citation described the integrated circuit as "the most important invention of our time." Kilby was 76. Robert Noyce, who died in 1990, was ineligible; Nobel prizes are not awarded posthumously. Texas Instruments had by then spent four decades building an institution on top of the foundational insight that owning the process — not merely the design — was the durable source of semiconductor competitive advantage. That conviction would animate every major strategic choice the company made for the following sixty-five years.

## Consumer Overreach and the Pivot to Analog, 1960–2000

The three decades following Kilby's invention saw Texas Instruments extend its process advantage into markets it ultimately could not hold. In the 1970s, TI moved aggressively into consumer electronics, introducing early electronic calculators and, in 1979, the TI-99/4A home computer. The consumer push reflected a genuine belief that semiconductor scale could overwhelm incumbents in any market that ran on silicon. The belief was partly correct and ultimately costly. Japanese electronics manufacturers — Casio in calculators, NEC and Fujitsu in DRAM memory — combined low-cost manufacturing with patient capital and systematically eroded TI's margins through the 1980s. By 1985, TI had absorbed losses in DRAM that threatened its financial stability; the consumer experiment had produced brand recognition but thin returns and a manufacturing footprint misaligned with the company's actual engineering strengths.

The strategic response required courage. Under CEO Jerry Junkins, and then under Tom Engibous after Junkins' sudden death in 1996, TI made the decision to exit commodity DRAM memory and refocus on two areas where it held genuine differentiation: digital signal processors and analog semiconductors. The exits were painful and expensive — fabs retooled, product lines wound down, thousands of employees affected. But the strategic logic was sound. DSPs and analog ICs served industrial, automotive, and communications customers who valued reliability, long product life cycles, and deep engineering support over the lowest possible unit price. These customers were structurally unlike consumer electronics buyers, and TI's incumbent engineering relationships gave it defensible positions that the company's Japanese competitors could not easily replicate.

## The Templeton Era and the Analog Consolidation, 2004–2023

Rich Templeton became chief executive officer in 2004 and spent nearly two decades executing the analog-and-industrial thesis with disciplined consistency. The most consequential single action of his tenure was the acquisition of National Semiconductor Corporation, announced April 4, 2011, for $6.5 billion in cash — ~~the largest acquisition in TI's history at the time~~ ==its largest deal since the roughly $7.6 billion Burr-Brown acquisition announced in 2000==. National Semiconductor was the second-largest analog IC company in the world, with particular strength in power management, a product category that TI had identified as structurally attractive because power management ICs are required in every electronic system and carry long design-in cycles that entrench incumbents. The PowerWise energy-management portfolio and National's precision analog catalogue roughly doubled TI's analog scale and established the combined company as the clear global leader in a fragmented but enormous market.

The Templeton era also required a difficult but ultimately correct withdrawal from mobile. TI's OMAP application processors powered early smartphones, including the original Motorola Droid, and represented a plausible path to leadership in mobile silicon. By 2012, however, Qualcomm had established an insurmountable position through baseband integration, and Apple's internal silicon design program had rendered merchant-market application processors architecturally inferior for premium handsets. Templeton's team announced in late 2012 that TI would exit OMAP entirely — absorbing short-term revenue loss and customer relationship costs to redirect engineering headcount and capital toward analog and embedded processing. The OMAP exit freed capacity, both financial and organizational, that was subsequently directed toward what became the 300mm analog fab program.

That program, conceived in earnest circa 2018–2020, was the capex commitment that would define TI's competitive trajectory through the 2030s. The economic logic was straightforward: 300mm wafers yield approximately 2.5 times as many die as 200mm wafers at comparable process cost, translating to unit cost reductions of 40% or more at full utilization. No other pure-analog IDM had completed this transition at scale. TI broke ground on SM1, the first 300mm fab at its Sherman, Texas mega-site, in May 2022.

## Succession and Execution, 2023–2026

Haviv Ilan assumed the chief executive role in May 2023, succeeding Templeton who had spent 45 years at TI, the final 19 as CEO. Ilan's profile differed from his predecessor's in background if not in strategic conviction: an Israeli-born engineer who had joined TI through the 2000 acquisition of Butterfly Communications, a wireless technology startup, he had spent the preceding three years as chief operating officer with direct oversight of manufacturing and sales. His elevation came precisely as the company entered the most demanding execution phase of its history — constructing multiple 300mm fabs simultaneously while navigating a severe industry-wide inventory correction that compressed revenue through 2023 and 2024.

The correction, TI's critics noted, was partly self-inflicted. The company had built capacity ahead of recoverable demand, and when post-pandemic destocking hit industrial customers in 2023, TI's fab utilization rates fell sharply while depreciation on newly operational equipment continued to accumulate. The episode validated the central risk that had shadowed the 300mm capex program from its inception: that a manufacturing-first strategy becomes a liability in downturns unless end demand ultimately catches up to the installed base.

By late 2025, SM1 in Sherman had begun production. In January 2026, Ilan added the chairmanship to his responsibilities when Templeton retired from the board entirely. Six weeks later, on February 4, 2026, TI announced the $7.5 billion all-cash acquisition of Silicon Laboratories — its largest acquisition since National Semiconductor, and the first major portfolio expansion under Ilan's independent leadership. Q1 2026 revenue of $4.83 billion, a 19% year-over-year increase, confirmed that the industrial recovery had arrived in force. Whether the Sherman mega-site, the Silicon Labs integration, and the $60 billion-plus capex commitment would compound into the durable free-cash-flow machine that Templeton had designed and Ilan had inherited to operate — that question would be answered across the decade ahead.

chapters.title: Two Segments, Six Markets: Analog, Embedded Processing, and the 100,000-Part Catalog Driving Customer Stickiness
chapters.body:
## The Catalog as Competitive Weapon

Texas Instruments does not compete by building the fastest chip or the most advanced process node. It competes by being everywhere. With more than 100,000 distinct part numbers spanning voltage ranges from sub-1V digital core rails to 600V motor drive circuits, TI's catalog operates as a kind of gravitational field—pulling system architects into its orbit at the design stage and keeping them there for the decade or more that a given product generation remains in production. The company's two reportable segments, Analog and Embedded Processing, are the twin pillars of that strategy, and understanding what each contains—and which end markets each one feeds—is essential to understanding why the company's revenue mix looks the way it does in fiscal 2025.

## Analog: The $14 Billion Engine

The Analog segment generated $14.01 billion in fiscal 2025, representing 79% of total company revenue. It encompasses two distinct product families: Power and Signal Chain.

Power is the faster-growing of the two, and arguably the most strategically important product line TI owns. The family spans DC/DC switching regulators in buck, boost, and buck-boost topologies; battery-management system (BMS) ICs for cell balancing and state-of-charge estimation; AC/DC and isolated DC/DC converters; load switches and power multiplexers; multi-phase controllers and integrated power stages; and gate drivers for silicon and silicon carbide transistors. The economic rationale for Power's growth is structural: electrification—in vehicles, in data centers, and across industrial systems—multiplies the number of conversion and regulation stages in any given system architecture, and each stage requires at least one TI IC.

The 48V power architecture transition in hyperscale data centers illustrates the dynamic with particular clarity. As AI accelerator clusters—GPU boards, TPU ASICs, custom silicon—demand hundreds of amps of current at sub-1V core rails, server architects have been pushed toward 48V bus voltages to reduce resistive losses in copper power delivery networks. That architectural shift created immediate demand for a new generation of high-voltage, high-efficiency DC/DC conversion ICs. TI's response included the [TPS1685](https://www.ti.com/product/TPS1685) 48V hot-swap eFuse, announced in March 2025, which combines overvoltage protection, inrush current limiting, and fault isolation in a single device for AI server power shelves. The TPS1685 is representative of a broader design push: TI's Power engineers have been targeting data-center infrastructure as a priority vertical, and it showed—data-center revenue grew approximately 90% year-over-year in Q1 2026.

The 300mm process node underpins TI's ability to compete on price as well as performance in Power ICs. Analog semiconductor manufacturing has historically run on 200mm (8-inch) wafers; most of TI's competitors—Analog Devices, Microchip, STMicroelectronics, NXP—continue to source meaningful portions of their analog production from 200mm fabs, either internally or through contract foundries. A 300mm wafer contains approximately 2.5 times the die area of a 200mm wafer at similar process cost, implying die cost reductions of 40% or more at comparable utilization. No other pure-analog IDM has achieved 300mm conversion at TI's scale, and the implication is that TI can profitably price Power ICs below the floor at which competitors can match without degrading their own margins. That cost asymmetry does not appear overnight—it materializes over years of utilization ramp—but it is the mechanism by which TI expects to extend its market share in commodity analog categories through the late 2020s.

Signal Chain, the second Analog sub-family, encompasses operational amplifiers, analog-to-digital converters (in SAR, delta-sigma, and pipeline architectures), digital-to-analog converters, interface ICs spanning RS-232, RS-485, CAN, LIN, USB, and high-speed SerDes protocols, isolation devices, current-sensing amplifiers, temperature sensors, and clocks and timing circuits. Signal Chain products are more heterogeneous and application-specific than Power; a delta-sigma ADC for a medical electrocardiogram system has different precision and noise specifications than a pipeline ADC for a software-defined radio, even if both appear in the same product catalog. TI's depth in Signal Chain derives from decades of accumulation: the company has been designing operational amplifiers since the late 1960s and has the application engineering resources to support extremely narrow vertical use cases—a capability that matters when a medical OEM needs a biosignal front-end IC qualified to IEC 60601 and supported by reference designs specific to their ECG electrode configuration.

## Embedded Processing: Real-Time Strength, Consumer Retreat

The Embedded Processing segment contributed $2.70 billion in fiscal 2025, roughly 15% of total revenue—a share that has compressed over the prior decade as TI deliberately exited high-volume consumer MCU markets in favor of defensible, high-mix positions in industrial and automotive applications. That strategic pruning left some revenue on the table and ceded share in general-purpose MCUs to STMicroelectronics and Microchip Technology, but it also concentrated the segment in markets where TI's real-time control expertise and functional-safety certifications constitute genuine differentiators.

The C2000 family is the clearest expression of that strategy. These real-time control MCUs are built around a proprietary 32-bit C28x core optimized for fixed-point and floating-point DSP operations at deterministic latencies—a profile that maps directly onto the control loops in solar inverters, industrial motor drives, EV charging stations, and switched-mode power supplies. The C2000 Piccolo sub-family, running at up to 120 MHz and integrating multiple PWM modules, analog comparators, and sigma-delta filter inputs, had accumulated design wins across virtually every major EV charging station architecture by 2025. When an EV driver plugs in at a Level 2 charger, the odds are substantial that a C2000 is managing the power factor correction and inverter gate drive in the wall unit. TI's position in this vertical is the product of two decades of application-specific silicon development, reference design investment, and customer enablement—not the kind of advantage that a new entrant with a commodity Cortex-M4 part can easily displace.

The automotive processor line addresses a different layer of the vehicle architecture. The Jacinto TDA4x series targets ADAS fusion and zone controller applications, providing heterogeneous compute fabrics—a combination of Arm Cortex-A cores for high-level processing, DSPs for sensor signal processing, and dedicated hardware accelerators for deep learning inference. These processors compete with NXP's S32 family and Renesas's R-Car line for the ECU designs that aggregate radar, camera, and lidar data into a coherent environment model. The TDA3x, a simpler variant, handles radar signal processing in the 77 GHz mmWave radar-on-chip ecosystem—a product line TI branded AWR for automotive and IWR for industrial sensing applications.

## Six Markets, Shifting Weights

| End Market | FY2025 Revenue Share | Primary Products | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|
| Industrial | ~~42%~~ ==33%== | Power ICs, Signal Chain, C2000, IWR radar | Recovering; grew >30% YoY in Q1 2026 |
| Automotive | ~~22%~~ ==33%== | Gate drivers, BMS, Jacinto, AWR radar | Secular growth from electrification |
| Personal Electronics | ~~15%~~ ==21%== | Power PMIC, USB-C controllers, audio | Flat to declining share; cyclical |
| Enterprise/Data Center | ~~10%~~ ==9%== | 48V converters, multi-phase controllers | Accelerating; ~90% YoY Q1 2026 |
| Communications | ~~6%~~ ==3%== | Signal Chain, power for 5G radio | Stable to declining |
| Other | ~~5%~~ ==~1%== | ~~DLP chipsets, calculator~~ ==Calculator== | Structural decline |

The directional story embedded in that table is TI's deliberate migration ~~away from personal electronics and communications—both characterized~~ ==away from communications and the long tail of legacy consumer-tethered businesses—characterized== by short product cycles, concentrated customer bases, and price pressure—toward industrial and automotive, where design-win cycles run two to five years, product lifetimes run a decade or more, and the analog content per system is growing, not shrinking. ==Industrial and automotive together now account for roughly two-thirds of revenue, with the two end markets running essentially tied at one-third each.== The industrial recovery from the 2023–2024 inventory correction confirmed that the underlying secular demand story remained intact: industrial revenue grew more than 30% year-over-year in Q1 2026, the strongest growth rate TI had reported for that end market in several years.

## The Silicon Labs Gap-Fill

The pending acquisition of Silicon Laboratories, announced February 4, 2026, at $231 per share and a total enterprise value of approximately $7.5 billion, addresses the one meaningful gap in TI's embedded product catalog: wireless connectivity for IoT endpoints. TI's existing SimpleLink portfolio covers Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, Thread, and Sub-GHz protocols—a capable lineup, but one that lacked the market-leading scale in Zigbee and Z-Wave that smart-home and smart-building system architects increasingly require as a single-vendor solution.

Silicon Labs' EFR32 multi-protocol SoC family is the flagship addition. The EFR32xG24, for example, supports concurrent Bluetooth, Zigbee, Thread, and Matter operation on a single die, with a software-defined radio front end that allows protocol switching without hardware modification—a capability that has made it the default choice for smart-building sensor node designers who need to support multiple protocol stacks across different customer deployments. The WGM, BGM, and MGM module families extend that connectivity in pre-certified RF modules, lowering the regulatory burden for customers who cannot afford their own FCC antenna testing. The combined TI-Silicon Labs catalog, once integrated, will cover essentially every wireless protocol relevant to industrial IoT, smart building, and smart home applications—positioning TI as the analog and connectivity one-stop shop for the building-automation OEMs that already depend on its Power and Signal Chain ICs for sensing and power conversion.

The manufacturing synergy case rests on migrating Silicon Labs' outsourced 8-inch foundry volumes onto TI's 300mm fabs after the deal closes, expected in the first half of 2027. TI's management has cited $450 million in annual synergies within three years post-close; a meaningful fraction of that figure depends on the 300mm cost advantage applying to wireless connectivity die as effectively as it applies to analog power ICs—an assumption that will require process development work but is consistent with the physics of the manufacturing cost equation. If it executes, the Silicon Labs acquisition becomes not merely a TAM expansion but a demonstration that TI's manufacturing strategy can absorb adjacent product families and structurally reprice them downward relative to outsourced competitors.

chapters.title: Revenue Recovery, Margin Compression, and the Free-Cash-Flow Inflection: TI's Financial Architecture, 2019–2026
chapters.body:
## The Cycle in Full: From $14 Billion to $20 Billion and Back

Texas Instruments entered 2019 as a company mid-transition — having exited its wireless baseband business earlier in the decade, it was reorienting every dollar of capital toward analog and embedded processing for industrial and automotive markets. Revenue that year stood at $14.38 billion, with operating income of $5.54 billion and a 38.5% operating margin reflecting the efficiency gains from that strategic simplification. The company was buying back stock aggressively and growing its dividend, and the analog-plus-internal-manufacturing thesis looked tidy and self-reinforcing.

Then the pandemic arrived, briefly disrupted demand, and then unleashed one of the most violent semiconductor upcycles in memory. TI's 2020 revenue dipped modestly to $14.46 billion before the whipsaw began. By 2021, revenue surged 27% to $18.34 billion as customers — startled by pandemic-era supply shortages — began ordering far beyond immediate need, building buffer inventory across automotive, industrial, and consumer channels. The Analog segment led the advance, as virtually every industrial and automotive system suddenly needed more power management and signal-chain content. Embedded Processing followed, driven by microcontroller supply tightness that elevated pricing across the board.

The peak arrived in 2022. Revenue reached $20.03 billion, the highest in TI's history, and gross margins crested above 67% — a figure that reflected both the pricing power of constrained supply and the absence of the underutilization charges that would dominate the conversation two years later. Operating income exceeded $9 billion, an operating margin above 45%. Management, to its credit, resisted the temptation to treat the peak as a new baseline.

The correction was severe. As customers recognized that their warehouses were overstocked, order cancellations cascaded across the supply chain. Revenue fell to $17.52 billion in 2023, a 13% decline, as industrial customers — TI's largest end market — bore the heaviest destocking. By 2024, the trough deepened further to $15.64 billion, a 22% retreat from the 2022 peak. The magnitude of the drop, concentrated in industrial and communications equipment, reflected not a loss of design wins but a classic inventory correction compounded by an extraordinarily long cycle of overbooking.

## Segment Anatomy: Analog's Lead and Embedded Processing's Lagging Recovery

The divergence between TI's two primary segments through the down-cycle reveals the underlying character of each business. The Analog segment — power management ICs, signal chain devices, and the 80,000-part catalog that sits embedded in virtually every piece of industrial electronics — proved more resilient in absolute terms but shed significant revenue from its peak nonetheless. By fiscal 2024, Analog revenue had fallen to approximately $12.19 billion before recovering to $14.01 billion in fiscal 2025, a 15% year-over-year gain that outpaced the overall company recovery.

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue | Analog Revenue | Embedded Processing Revenue | Operating Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 | $14.38B | ~$10.6B | ~$2.8B | 38.5% |
| 2021 | $18.34B | ~$13.8B | ~$3.5B | 42.9% |
| 2022 | $20.03B | ~$15.0B | ~$3.7B | ~45% |
| 2023 | $17.52B | ~$13.1B | ~$3.1B | ~36% |
| 2024 | $15.64B | $12.19B | $2.55B | ~~29%~~ ==~35%== |
| 2025 | $17.68B | $14.01B | $2.70B | 34.1% |
| Q1 2026 | $4.83B | — | — | — |

Embedded Processing's recovery was more hesitant. The segment — encompassing the C2000 real-time control MCUs, Sitara applications processors, Hercules safety MCUs, Jacinto ADAS processors, and SimpleLink wireless connectivity — reached only $2.70 billion in 2025, a 6% year-over-year gain that still left it well below its 2022 peak. Management acknowledged ongoing competitive pressure from Renesas, STMicroelectronics, and NXP in certain MCU categories, and the segment has been the subject of internal restructuring aimed at focusing resources on higher-margin embedded families. The pending Silicon Labs acquisition substantially enlarges the wireless connectivity portion of what TI will eventually report under Embedded Processing.

## Gross Margin Compression and the Underutilization Tax

The margin story from 2022 to 2024 is the story of a deliberate strategic choice meeting the worst possible timing. Texas Instruments made the decision to equip its new 300mm fabs — RFAB2 in Dallas, LFAB in Lehi, and SM1 in Sherman — ahead of demand, committing billions in tooling and clean-room infrastructure before the revenue base existed to absorb the associated fixed costs. When revenue fell 22% from peak to trough while depreciation and fixed manufacturing costs surged, the arithmetic was punishing.

Gross margin declined from above 67% in 2022 to an estimated 57–59% range at the 2024 trough — a compression of approximately eight to ten percentage points. On a $15.64 billion revenue base, each percentage point of gross margin represents roughly $156 million. At peak underutilization, TI was absorbing charges that management characterized as the direct cost of running partially loaded fabs, a headwind that suppressed operating income by an estimated $1.3–1.5 billion annually relative to what the same revenue would have generated at prior utilization levels. Operating margin compressed from the 45% peak to ~~approximately 29%~~ ==approximately 35%== in 2024, an impairment that, had TI chosen to be a pure-play fabless designer, would simply not have existed.

~~The recovery in 2025 — operating margin back to 34.1% — partially reflected the return of revenue volume but more directly reflected the gradual improvement in fab utilization as SM1 began production in late 2025 and LFAB continued ramping.~~ ==2025 operating margin held essentially flat at 34.1% even as revenue grew 13%, as the cost of bringing SM1 online in late 2025 and continued equipping at LFAB offset the utilization benefits of the higher volume base.== Management's target of returning to 65%-plus gross margins by 2027–2028 rests on the thesis that each percentage point recovered on $18–20 billion in revenue adds $180–200 million to operating income. The trajectory is not guaranteed; it requires both sustained demand growth and disciplined capital allocation against the remaining equipping phases of the Sherman and Lehi programs.

## The Capex Super-Cycle in Numbers

The scale of TI's capital investment program is without precedent in the company's history and has few analogs among large-cap semiconductor manufacturers outside of TSMC and Intel. [Texas Instruments 10-K, filed February 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000097476/000009747626000059/txn-20251231.htm) disclosed capital expenditures of $4.55 billion in fiscal 2025, following $4.82 billion in 2024, $4.98 billion in 2023, and $4.64 billion in 2022. Against TI's pre-program historical capex run-rate of approximately $1.5–2.0 billion annually, the company has been spending more than double its prior normalized investment level for four consecutive years.

| Year | Revenue | Capex | Capex/Revenue | FCF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019–2021 avg. | ~$15.7B | ~$1.8B | ~11% | ~$5.0B+ |
| 2022 | $20.03B | $4.64B | 23.2% | ~$5.6B |
| 2023 | $17.52B | $4.98B | 28.4% | ~$1.7B |
| 2024 | $15.64B | $4.82B | 30.8% | $1.50B |
| 2025 | $17.68B | $4.55B | 25.7% | $2.94B |

The capex-as-percentage-of-revenue figure — 25–31% through 2023–2025 versus a historical norm closer to 5–10% — explains almost entirely why free cash flow collapsed even as the underlying business retained significant earnings power. The depreciation lag embedded in these numbers is the mechanism by which the long-run cost advantage accrues: the equipment being installed in Sherman and Lehi today will depreciate over ~~25–30~~ ==5–10== years, ~~creating a fixed cost base whose denominator grows as volume fills the capacity~~ ==front-loading the fixed cost base in the years before volume fully fills the capacity==. ~~A fab that costs $10 billion to build and operates for 30 years generates cost amortization of roughly $333 million annually;~~ ==Equipment costing $10 billion generates roughly $1.0–2.0 billion of annual cost amortization during the depreciation window;== ~~as~~ ==once that drag rolls off and== that same fab runs at 90% utilization producing chips with unit costs 40% below 200mm equivalents, the economics become transformative.

## The FCF Inflection and Management's 25–35% Target

~~The 2025 free cash flow result — $2.94 billion, or 16.6% of revenue — was the clearest financial signal since the cycle turned that TI's strategy is beginning to work as the model predicted.~~ ==FY2025 free cash flow of $2.94 billion (16.6% of revenue), followed by a climb in trailing-12-month FCF to $4.35 billion once Q1 2026 reported, was the clearest financial signal since the cycle turned that TI's strategy is beginning to work as the model predicted.== Operating cash flow reached $7.15 billion, with the gap to FCF representing the $4.55 billion capex program. The near-doubling of FCF from the $1.50 billion (9.6%) 2024 figure reflects both the revenue recovery and a modest capex step-down, and the trajectory into 2026 looks favorable: management guided Q2 revenue to $5.0–5.4 billion, a range that implies full-year 2026 revenue of $19–20 billion if sequential momentum holds.

Management's stated long-run FCF/revenue target of 25–35% implies $4.5–6.3 billion of annual free cash flow at an $18–19 billion normalized revenue base. The arithmetic path is straightforward: every $500 million reduction in annual capex from the $4.55 billion 2025 level contributes approximately $400–450 million to FCF after the tax shield on depreciation. A capex normalization from $4.55 billion to $2.5–3.0 billion — achievable by 2027–2028 once SM1 and LFAB2 complete their equipping phases — releases $1.5–2.0 billion in annual FCF. Layered onto revenue growth toward $19–20 billion and margin expansion from improved utilization, the lower end of the 25–35% target becomes visible in a base-case scenario by 2027–2028. The bear case — demand disappointment keeping utilization rates below 70% into 2027, or Silicon Labs integration costs running above plan — delays the inflection by two to three years without changing the eventual destination.

## Balance Sheet Architecture and the Silicon Labs Leverage Equation

At December 31, 2025, TI carried $13.55 billion in long-term debt against $4.88 billion in cash and short-term investments, implying net debt of approximately $8.67 billion. Stockholders' equity of $16.27 billion produced a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.83 times. Against estimated EBITDA of approximately $7.5–8.0 billion, leverage stood at roughly 1.1 times net debt to EBITDA — a conservative position for an A/A2-rated industrial technology company.

The Silicon Labs acquisition changes that calculus materially. The $7.5 billion all-cash transaction, financed through TI's remaining cash and investment-grade debt issuance ahead of the expected H1 2027 close, will increase gross debt to approximately $19–21 billion. Cash balances, which already declined from $7.58 billion at year-end 2024 to $4.88 billion at year-end 2025 as the company funded shareholder returns in excess of earnings, will be substantially further depleted. On a pro-forma basis, net debt rises toward $15–17 billion and gross leverage approaches 2.0–2.2 times EBITDA — still investment-grade, but materially tighter than the pre-acquisition structure. Interest coverage, currently approximately 7–8 times on an EBIT-to-interest basis, compresses toward 4–6 times in the immediate post-close period, reducing the financial flexibility that has historically allowed TI to sustain dividend growth through cycles.

## Capital Returns: The Arithmetic Tension

Texas Instruments has raised its dividend for ~~21~~ ==22== consecutive years through 2026, a streak that functions as both a strategic signal and a commitment device. In fiscal 2025, dividends consumed $5.00 billion and share repurchases an additional $1.48 billion, for total capital returns of $6.48 billion — a figure that exceeded net income of $5.00 billion by approximately 30% and required balance-sheet drawdown to fund.

> "Our objective is to return all free cash flow to owners," management has reiterated across successive earnings calls, framing the excess-of-earnings return as a deliberate signaling exercise during a period when the capex cycle temporarily suppresses reported FCF below the long-run potential.

The tension is real and arithmetically visible. TI is simultaneously undertaking the largest acquisition in its history, running a capital expenditure program at 25% of revenue, and returning capital in excess of what it earns. The resolution of that tension depends entirely on whether the FCF inflection toward 25–35% of revenue materializes on the timelines management has described. If it does, the dividend growth streak extends, the Silicon Labs debt is progressively repaid, and the manufacturing thesis generates the compounding per-share value that has been the explicit promise of a decade of strategic investment. If the industrial recovery stalls or the integration disappoints, TI may face the first dividend coverage question in more than two decades — a scenario that would test the credibility of the entire financial architecture Haviv Ilan inherited and now owns.

chapters.title: Pricing the Inflection: TXN's Multiples, Historical Range, Peer Benchmarks, and Intrinsic-Value Scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Stretched Multiple on a Recovering Earnings Base

At $325 per share and a market capitalisation of approximately $290 billion, Texas Instruments entered the late-May 2026 freeze window as one of the most richly valued large-cap semiconductor companies in the world by nearly every conventional metric. The trailing twelve-month price-to-earnings multiple stood at roughly 54 times—a figure that reflected the asymmetry between the stock's near-80% rally over the prior 52 weeks and the still-recovering earnings base beneath it. The forward P/E on next-twelve-months consensus EPS compressed the picture only modestly, to approximately 38 times, while EV/EBITDA sat at roughly 34 times and EV/Sales at 16 times against an enterprise value of approximately $298 billion. Price-to-book of roughly 17 times completed a tableau of expansion-era multiples that, on their face, demanded explanation.

The explanation required a detour through history. During the decade spanning 2012 to 2022, TXN typically traded in a 20-to-30 times forward P/E band—a range that reflected the market's appreciation for the company's dividend consistency and analog-cycle exposure but not a structural manufacturing premium. The inventory correction of 2023-2024 compressed that band back toward 20 times as earnings troughed. The re-rating from roughly $170 to $325 was therefore not a simple earnings recovery but a wholesale narrative shift: the market chose to value TI not as a cyclical analog semiconductor company but as a manufacturing compounder with a durable cost moat and a decade of free-cash-flow inflection ahead of it. Haviv Ilan had framed TI's value proposition through a single phrase—"free cash flow per share growth"—and the market had chosen to believe it before the FCF had fully arrived.

## Peer-Group Multiples: Premium Justified or Priced for Perfection

Whether that re-rating was warranted depended in part on whether TI's premium over analog peers reflected structural differentiation or cycle timing. The comparison below captured the competitive landscape as of late May 2026.

| Company | Fwd P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Sales | P/B | NTM Rev. Growth |
|---------|---------|-----------|----------|-----|-----------------|
| **TXN** | ~38x | ~34x | ~16x | ~17x | ~20% |
| **ADI** | ~28x | ~22x | ~10x | ~3x | ~12% |
| **MCHP** | ~18x | ~15x | ~5x | ~4x | ~8% |
| **NXPI** | ~19x | ~14x | ~5x | ~3x | ~10% |
| **IFNNY** | ~22x | ~13x | ~3x | ~2x | ~9% |
| **STM** | ~16x | ~10x | ~2x | ~1.5x | ~6% |

*Approximate figures; peer multiples derived from market consensus as of the May 2026 frozen snapshot.*

The discount at which every peer traded against TXN reflected identifiable structural differences rather than simple relative undervaluation. Analog Devices, the closest comparator by business model, carried a forward P/E of roughly 28 times—a spread of 10 multiple turns that acknowledged TI's larger revenue base and manufacturing differentiation while embedding a risk premium for the Silicon Labs integration complexity. Microchip Technology and NXP Semiconductors each traded in the high-teens to low-twenties on forward earnings, weighed down by heavier exposure to automotive inventory cycles, elevated net debt on Microchip's balance sheet from prior acquisitions, and foundry-dependent manufacturing models that offered less structural cost optionality than TI's integrated device manufacturer approach. STMicroelectronics, at roughly 16 times forward earnings and a single-digit EV/Sales, reflected persistent skepticism about European industrial demand alongside the company's slower progress in converting its manufacturing base to more economical geometries. Infineon's mid-range multiple captured genuine power-semiconductor leadership in automotive and industrial applications, offset by headwinds from the same European industrial recession that pressured STM.

## Scenario Architecture: The Three Paths

The widest range of outcomes in TI's valuation story ran through a single variable: free cash flow per share in the 2028-2029 window. Management's stated long-run FCF/revenue framework of 25-35% provided the goalposts; the debate was over when and at what revenue level TI reached that target.

| Scenario | 2029 FCF | FCF/Rev | Revenue | Capex | Multiple | Price Target |
|----------|----------|---------|---------|-------|----------|--------------|
| **Bull** | $6.0B+ | ~28% | ~$22B | ~$2.5B | 30x FCF | ~$200+ |
| **Base** | $4.5B | ~23% | ~$19.5B | ~$3.0B | 25x FCF | ~$125 |
| **Bear** | $3.0B | ~17% | ~$18B | ~$3.5B | 20x FCF | ~$65 |

*Per-share price targets based on approximately 900 million diluted shares; FCF multiples reflect scenario-specific risk premiums.*

The bull case required four conditions to align: capital expenditure normalising to $2.5 billion by 2027 as SM1 equipping peaked; industrial and automotive revenue growing 8-10% annually through 2029 on the back of electrification tailwinds; the Silicon Labs acquisition delivering its full $450 million synergy run-rate by year three post-close through migration of outsourced foundry volumes onto TI's 300mm fabs; and data-centre power management sustaining its hypergrowth trajectory. On those assumptions, a 30 times FCF multiple—analogous to what the market had historically awarded TSMC or ASML for structural irreplaceability—would support a price above $200. The critical observation was that even the bull case implied meaningful downside from $325.

The base case assumed more measured execution: capex declining to $3 billion by 2028 rather than 2027, revenue reaching approximately $19.5 billion on blended 7-8% annual growth, and Silicon Labs delivering partial synergies—perhaps $200-250 million of the $450 million target—by 2028. Free cash flow of $4.5 billion at 25 times implied approximately $125 per share, a discount of more than 60% to the May 2026 price.

The bear case required no catastrophe, only accumulated friction: capital expenditure remaining stubbornly elevated at $3.5 billion through 2028 because industrial demand recovery disappointed, Silicon Labs integration incurring material one-time costs and disruption, and European and Chinese industrial demand growing at only 3-4% annually. Free cash flow of $3 billion at 20 times implied approximately $65 per share.

## What $325 Embeds: The Implied FCF Assumption

At $325 and a market capitalisation of approximately $290 billion, TXN's trailing FCF yield ~~barely registered at 1%—$2.94 billion of fiscal 2025 FCF against the market cap~~ ==stood at approximately 1.5%—$4.35 billion of trailing-twelve-month FCF through the Q1 2026 print against the market cap==. Closing the gap between that yield and any conventional institutional threshold required projecting forward to a period in which FCF was dramatically higher. Working backwards from the market price: ~~assuming a 10% FCF yield as a minimum long-term return threshold, the market was implicitly pricing approximately $7-8 billion of annual FCF for the 2028-2030 period at a roughly 10 times multiple—an embedded FCF/revenue ratio of 38-42% at a $19-21 billion revenue base.~~ ==even if the market were underwriting $7-8 billion of annual FCF for the 2028-2030 period, capitalising that stream against the current $290 billion equity value implied a 35-40 times forward FCF multiple and a 2.5-3% forward yield—well below any conventional long-term return threshold—on an embedded FCF/revenue ratio of 38-42% at a $19-21 billion revenue base.==

That implied ratio sat materially above management's own stated upper bound of 35%, and represented a scenario that required not only flawless capex normalization but also the high end of the demand recovery trajectory. The market, in other words, was pricing in a best-of-all-worlds outcome in which the $60-billion manufacturing programme delivered its cost advantages precisely on schedule, Silicon Labs added FCF rather than consuming it during integration, and industrial demand grew without interruption throughout the normalization phase.

## DCF Bounds: Three Stages, Two WACCs

A three-stage discounted cash flow model captured the structural shape of TI's FCF trajectory: an elevated-capex phase spanning 2026-2027 in which FCF expanded modestly as revenue grew faster than capital expenditure; a normalization phase from 2028 through 2030 in which capex stepped down toward $2.5-3 billion and FCF inflected toward the 25-35% framework; and a steady state from 2031 onward in which FCF grew at approximately 4-5% annually in line with industrial and automotive secular demand growth.

Using a weighted average cost of capital of 8.5-9.5%—reflecting TI's A/A2 investment-grade credit rating, an equity beta of approximately 1.0-1.1, and the execution risk embedded in the capex programme and Silicon Labs integration—the sensitivity table below bounded the intrinsic value range on the base-case FCF trajectory.

| WACC \ Terminal Growth | 3.0% | 4.0% | 5.0% |
|------------------------|------|------|------|
| **8.5%** | ~$155 | ~$185 | ~$230 |
| **9.0%** | ~$135 | ~$160 | ~$195 |
| **9.5%** | ~$115 | ~$140 | ~$165 |

*Per-share intrinsic value; base-case FCF trajectory assumes $4.5 billion FCF by 2028, normalising capex, growing at terminal rate from 2031.*

The table delivered a consistent message: at any reasonable discount rate and any terminal growth rate below 5%, base-case DCF mathematics implied intrinsic value well below the May 2026 market price. Only a 5% terminal growth rate at an 8.5% WACC produced a value approaching $230—still a 30% discount to $325. Bridging to the current stock price without implausible assumptions required either bull-case FCF (above $6 billion by 2029) or a discount rate below 8%, which would assign TI a sub-utility cost of capital for a business with meaningful cyclicality and a multi-year integration overhang.

## The Re-Rating Thesis: Compounder Premium or Cycle Fiction

The market had rendered an early verdict. At 38 times forward earnings, it assigned Texas Instruments a valuation closer to a compounding infrastructure business than to a cyclical semiconductor producer. The underlying thesis was coherent: if the 300mm manufacturing strategy executed as designed, TI would possess a structural unit-cost advantage against every analog competitor reliant on contract foundries—an advantage that would compound as TI filled its fabs and peers faced rising foundry pricing in a capacity-constrained world. The Silicon Labs acquisition, if integrated cleanly, expanded the serviceable market into wireless IoT connectivity and added a second secular growth vector atop the industrial and automotive base.

But the path from current valuations to validated execution spanned approximately three to five years of simultaneous success across capex management, industrial demand recovery, acquisition integration, and balance-sheet normalization. During that interval, the stock's embedded assumptions left virtually no margin for moderate disappointment. Analog peers—ADI, Microchip, NXP—all traded at multiples that priced less credit for the structural thesis but offered correspondingly greater margin of safety. For the market's current multiple to prove conservative rather than optimistic, Texas Instruments would need to become the TSMC of analog: not merely a good semiconductor company, but a structurally irreplaceable one whose manufacturing scale and cost discipline compelled competitors to price below cost or cede market share. That outcome was possible. As of the May 2026 frozen window, it had not yet been demonstrated.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: The Analog Inventory Cycle, Management Commentary, and the Confirmed Turn in 2025–2026
chapters.body:
## The Descent and the Trough

Few industrial cycles in modern semiconductor history matched the severity of the analog inventory correction that ran from late 2022 through the first half of 2024. At the cycle's apex, Texas Instruments generated quarterly revenue approaching five billion dollars; by Q1 2024, that figure had compressed to approximately $3.66 billion—a decline of roughly 25 percent over six quarters that squeezed gross margins from above 67 percent toward 57 to 59 percent and forced management into the uncomfortable position of defending an accelerating $60 billion fab commitment while dividend payments were on course to exceed net income.

The correction had a mechanical cause. Customers across TI's industrial and automotive supply chains had over-ordered during the 2021–2022 shortage era, building safety stocks calibrated for a world where chips were perpetually scarce. When end-demand softened, the excess inventory took time to burn through. A brief stabilization in Q3 2023 around $4.5 billion gave way to renewed weakness in Q4 2023 and into early 2024, as customers reduced orders further rather than risk additional build.

Haviv Ilan, who assumed the CEO role in May 2023 near the cycle's midpoint, found himself defending TI's manufacturing-first strategy at each successive trough quarter. On the Q4 2023 earnings call in January 2024—with revenue having compressed to approximately $4.25 billion and analysts pressing on the logic of accelerating capital investment into a weak market—Ilan was unequivocal. "Our investments are consistent with our long-term outlook for our market," he told analysts, framing the capex program as a decade-long commitment to unit-cost leadership rather than a cycle bet. Rafael Lizardi, the chief financial officer, reinforced the capital-return message: the quarterly dividend would continue growing, as it had for 20 consecutive years, underpinned by the conviction that trough earnings were a temporary rather than structural phenomenon. The framework, consistent across every call of the downturn period, was that current net income was the wrong denominator for assessing TI's capital return capacity; the binding constraint was long-run free cash flow.

## The YoY Inflection: Q1 2025

The first confirmed year-over-year revenue growth arrived in Q1 2025, when TI reported approximately $4.07 billion against Q1 2024's $3.66 billion trough—an 11 percent improvement that signaled the destocking cycle had largely cleared in the industrial segment. The sequential path through fiscal 2025 confirmed the recovery: revenue moved from $4.07 billion in Q1 through progressively stronger quarters, reaching approximately $4.43 billion in Q4 2025, a trajectory that lifted [full-year revenue to $17.68 billion](https://investor.ti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/ti-reports-q4-2025-and-2025-financial-results-and-shareholder), up 13 percent over fiscal 2024's $15.64 billion trough.

The recovery was not uniform across TI's two operating segments. The Analog segment—generating [$14.01 billion in fiscal 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000097476/000009747626000059/txn-20251231.htm)—grew revenue 15 percent year-over-year as power management and signal chain products benefited from industrial restocking and new demand in data-center power management. Embedded Processing's recovery was materially more muted: fiscal 2025 revenue of $2.70 billion represented only 6 percent improvement year-over-year, reflecting pricing pressure in the microcontroller market and share erosion in certain automotive embedded applications where competitors had made inroads during the downturn. Embedded Processing, which had contributed roughly 20 percent of TI's revenue at the 2022 peak, had shrunk to approximately 15 percent of mix by 2025.

| Segment | FY2024 Revenue | FY2025 Revenue | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Analog | ~$12.18B | $14.01B | +15% |
| Embedded Processing | ~$2.55B | $2.70B | +6% |
| Other | ~$0.91B | $0.97B | +7% |
| **Total** | **$15.64B** | **$17.68B** | **+13%** |

## Q1 2026: The Confirmation

If Q1 2025 marked the inflection, Q1 2026 delivered the confirmation that the recovery was durable and broad-based. On April 22, 2026, TI reported first-quarter revenue of $4.83 billion, up 19 percent year-over-year and 9 percent sequentially, beating the top of prior guidance by approximately $150 million. The detail beneath the headline was arguably more significant than the aggregate number.

Industrial revenue grew more than 30 percent year-over-year, the largest absolute contributor to the beat. On the Q1 2026 earnings call, Ilan told analysts that the industrial strength reflected three converging forces: channel restocking as inventory days normalized from excess levels, genuine end-demand growth in factory automation and energy infrastructure, and incremental share gains from design wins that had been awarded during the downturn and were now ramping to production volumes. The distinction between these drivers matters considerably for assessing how durable the recovery proves. Restocking is by definition transient—once channel inventories reach target days, the ordering impulse extinguishes. End-demand growth tied to industrial electrification is structural and multi-year. Share gains are sticky, provided TI's cost structure and technical support sustain the wins through product life cycles measured in decades. Ilan's commentary was careful to emphasize that the breadth and diversity of the industrial recovery—spanning factory automation, building systems, grid infrastructure, and medical—pointed toward structural rather than purely cyclical demand, a framing designed to reassure investors skeptical that the industrial upturn was simply a re-stocking artifact.

Data-center revenue grew approximately 90 percent year-over-year, driven by 48V bus architecture adoption in AI accelerator rack deployments at hyperscalers. TI's power management ICs—DC/DC converters, gate drivers, and point-of-load regulators—are embedded in the power delivery path for GPU and custom AI chip infrastructure at every major cloud operator. This was not a category that appeared prominently in TI's end-market commentary two years earlier; its emergence as a growth vector reflects both the magnitude of the AI infrastructure buildout and TI's preexisting analog portfolio depth in high-current, high-efficiency power conversion.

Automotive was approximately flat year-over-year, with management flagging a notable geographic split: China-based automotive customers remained cautious amid ongoing inventory uncertainty in the Chinese electric-vehicle market, while rest-of-world automotive was growing. Lizardi noted on the call that rest-of-world automotive content-per-vehicle trends remained intact, underscoring that the China softness was a regional demand issue rather than a structural challenge to TI's automotive positioning.

## Q2 2026 Guidance and the Revenue Peak Implication

Management's Q2 2026 guidance—revenue of $5.0 to $5.4 billion with diluted EPS of $1.77 to $2.05—carried specific historical significance. The midpoint of $5.2 billion would represent TI's strongest quarterly revenue since the 2022 cycle peak, and the guidance midpoint cleared analyst consensus by more than 7 percent at the time of issuance. Combining Q1 actuals of $4.83 billion with a Q2 midpoint of $5.2 billion implies first-half 2026 revenue of approximately $10.0 billion. If the second half maintains comparable sequential momentum—Q3 is historically TI's strongest seasonal quarter—full-year 2026 revenue could approach or exceed $21 billion, a new absolute peak and a meaningful validation of management's manufacturing-cost-reduction thesis. At the Q2 EPS midpoint of $1.91, a comparable sequential extrapolation for the second half implies full-year 2026 diluted EPS in the range of $7.50 to $8.00—approaching a near-doubling from fiscal 2024's trough and consistent with the operating leverage recovery management had projected consistently during the downturn period.

## The Dividend as a Signal

~~Texas Instruments raised its quarterly dividend to $1.36 per share in 2025, from $1.30 in 2024, extending a consecutive-annual-increase streak that reached 21 years by May 2026.~~ ==By the May 2026 snapshot, Texas Instruments' operative quarterly dividend stood at $1.42 per share, extending a consecutive-annual-increase streak that reached 22 years.== The signal embedded in this increase was deliberate and pointed. TI's total dividend payments of $5.00 billion in fiscal 2025 approximately equaled net income of $5.00 billion—a payout ratio of essentially 100 percent—requiring drawdown of the balance sheet to fund the gap. Cash and short-term investments declined to $4.88 billion at year-end 2025 from $7.58 billion a year earlier.

Management has been consistent about the rationale across multiple earnings calls. The binding constraint on TI's capital return is not current net income, which is temporarily depressed by depreciation charges on underutilized 300mm fabs, but long-run free cash flow. Lizardi articulated on the Q4 2025 call that TI's long-run financial model targets free cash flow margins of 25 to 35 percent of revenue; at a normalized $18 to $20 billion revenue base, that framework implies $4.5 to $7 billion of annual free cash flow—a level at which the current dividend is covered multiple times and buybacks can resume without balance-sheet erosion. The dividend increase, in this context, is less a financial decision than a communications act: management's statement to shareholders that the capital allocation framework remains intact and that trough earnings do not define the long-run capital return capacity of the business. ~~Twenty-one~~ ==Twenty-two== years of consecutive increases, sustained through the 2008 financial crisis, the 2020 pandemic quarter, and a two-year inventory correction that cut revenue by 25 percent, establish a credibility baseline that no single-quarter earnings result can readily impair.

## Earnings Quality

The relationship between TI's operating cash flow and reported net income in fiscal 2025 provides one of the cleaner earnings quality tests available in the semiconductor sector. [Operating cash flow of $7.15 billion](https://investor.ti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/ti-reports-q4-2025-and-2025-financial-results-and-shareholder) against net income of $5.00 billion implies a cash conversion ratio of approximately 1.43 times—$1.43 of cash from operations for every dollar of reported net income. The primary driver is non-cash depreciation and amortization on the fab program, which reduces reported earnings while TI incurs the actual cash cost through the capital expenditure line. This structure does not inflate earnings relative to cash flow; it does the opposite, producing a conservative income statement relative to underlying cash generation.

The Q4 2025 earnings release flagged a one-time charge reducing diluted EPS by approximately six cents, related to a restructuring item; underlying quarterly EPS absent this charge would have been modestly higher, though the magnitude was too small to alter the trajectory materially. More consequential for forward modeling is the treatment of underutilization charges. As TI's new 300mm fabs ramp toward higher utilization through 2026–2028, idle-capacity costs previously expensed will convert to lower per-unit cost of goods sold, creating a gross-margin tailwind that benefits reported earnings without any change in underlying cash economics. Analysts who project TI's forward earnings by mechanically applying current margin rates to forward revenue will systematically underestimate the margin expansion that accompanies volume-driven fab utilization improvement—precisely the dynamic that overstated the margin compression during the downturn and will overstate the recovery speed on the way up.

chapters.title: Haviv Ilan, Rafael Lizardi, and the Board: Engineering Discipline as Competitive Strategy
chapters.body:
## An Engineer at the Top

Haviv Ilan is an unusual figure in the Fortune 500 semiconductor world: a chief executive who joined his company as a junior engineer, never left, and arrived at the corner office after 24 years of accumulated institutional knowledge. Born in Israel in 1968, Ilan came to Texas Instruments in 1999 not through a headhunter or a lateral corporate move but through an acquisition. His employer, Butterfly Communications, was an Israeli wireless technology startup whose technology TI absorbed as part of its push into wireless connectivity ICs. Ilan joined the Ra'anana, Israel design center that TI maintained as one of its key analog and wireless engineering hubs, and he stayed.

Over the following two decades, Ilan progressed from engineering roles into wireless business unit leadership, eventually becoming general manager and director of engineering for the Ra'anana center—the facility that would become TI's center of gravity for Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and low-power connectivity silicon. In 2020, [TI named him executive vice president and chief operating officer](https://investor.ti.com/corporate-governance/leadership), giving him responsibility for worldwide business and sales organizations, technology and manufacturing operations, and IT. When Rich Templeton stepped back to executive chairman in May 2023, Ilan assumed the presidency and CEO role. In January 2026, following Templeton's full retirement after 45 years, Ilan consolidated both roles and became chairman of the board as well.

That biography matters for more than symbolism. Ilan is the first TI CEO born outside the United States, and his technical roots in wireless and mixed-signal IC design give him an engineer's credibility inside a company whose culture has always privileged engineering judgment over financial engineering. His familiarity with the Ra'anana design center also illuminates one dimension of the Silicon Labs acquisition logic: Ilan spent his formative TI years in connectivity silicon, and the $7.5 billion deal announced in February 2026 is in part a bet that TI can build a world-class wireless IoT franchise around the same product architecture he helped design.

## Continuation or Evolution: The Templeton Legacy

Rich Templeton's 19-year tenure as CEO produced two decisions that define TI's modern competitive position. The first was the $6.5 billion acquisition of National Semiconductor in 2011, which added roughly 12,000 analog SKUs, a manufacturing footprint that TI subsequently upgraded, and a power-management catalog that deepened TI's penetration of the industrial and communications end markets. The second was the deliberate exit from OMAP mobile applications processors in 2012 and 2013, a business TI had built into a temporary smartphone powerhouse, but which Templeton concluded was incompatible with TI's analog gross-margin profile and capital-intensity requirements. Together, those moves set TI on an industrial-and-automotive-first trajectory with a 300mm manufacturing cost thesis at its core.

Ilan has not revised that framework. He has extended it. The continued construction of Sherman SM1 through SM4, the Lehi LFAB2 expansion, the CHIPS Act funding agreement for up to $1.6 billion in direct support, and the $60-plus billion multi-decade capex commitment all represent execution within the Templeton blueprint rather than a strategic departure from it. Where Ilan has added his own convictions is in two areas: the wireless connectivity expansion through Silicon Labs, and a more explicit articulation of the data-center power opportunity—AI accelerator infrastructure demand that Templeton did not fully anticipate when framing the industrial-and-automotive thesis in the early 2010s.

Whether Ilan's Silicon Labs decision constitutes evolution or overcorrection remains contested. His critics argue that a $7.5 billion premium for a fabless connectivity IC company—with a deal multiple implying confidence in synergies that will take years to materialize—is a departure from the capital discipline that defined the Templeton era. His defenders note that Templeton also paid a meaningful premium for National Semiconductor and was vindicated over time. The difference is that the National deal deepened TI's core analog catalog; the Silicon Labs deal extends into an adjacent category with distinct engineering and competitive dynamics.

## Rafael Lizardi: West Point Discipline, Free-Cash-Flow Theology

CFO Rafael Lizardi joined Texas Instruments in 2001 through TI's finance development program and has served as chief financial officer since February 2017, making him one of the longer-tenured CFOs in the large-cap semiconductor sector. His background before TI is distinctive: a West Point engineering graduate and former U.S. Army Corps of Engineers officer, Lizardi brought a capital-planning discipline to TI's finance function that predates and arguably shapes the 300mm manufacturing commitment. Before his CFO appointment, he served as TI's corporate controller—a role that gave him visibility into every line of the manufacturing cost structure.

Lizardi's public financial communication has been built around a single metric: free cash flow per share. At virtually every earnings call and investor conference, his framing of TI's value proposition returns to a long-run FCF/revenue target of 25–35% and to the per-share growth trajectory that capital returns amplify. That framework disciplines how management discusses capex: elevated depreciation charges in the near term are not a margin problem to explain away but a deferred cost advantage to be redeemed when utilization rises. ~~In fiscal 2025, free cash flow nearly doubled to $2.94 billion, representing 16.6% of revenue—still well below the long-run target, but recovering from $1.50 billion in 2024 as capital expenditures declined slightly to $4.55 billion.~~ ==As of the May 2026 snapshot, with Q1 2026 already reported, TI's trailing-twelve-month free cash flow had reached $4.35 billion—still below the long-run target, but a marked step up from the $2.94 billion delivered in fiscal 2025 and the $1.50 billion delivered in fiscal 2024 as the capex super-cycle began working past its peak intensity.==

The Silicon Labs acquisition tests Lizardi's framework in ways that short-run EPS metrics obscure. Management guided that the deal would be accretive to earnings per share in the first full year after close—a statement calibrated to the financial community's near-term focus. But EPS accretion is consistent with poor long-run FCF outcomes if the $450 million synergy target slips, integration costs exceed estimates, or the debt service from the all-cash transaction dampens capital-return capacity. The FCF-per-share framework is the right lens through which to evaluate the deal, and Lizardi himself has framed it that way publicly. Whether the board holds management accountable to that standard over a multi-year horizon is the governance question.

## Board Composition and Institutional Patience

TI's board of directors is majority-independent with no significant activist or private equity representation. Major institutional shareholders—[Vanguard at approximately 8%, BlackRock at approximately 6%, State Street at approximately 4%](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000097476&type=DEF+14A)—hold passive index positions whose governance posture is effectively deferential to management except in extreme circumstances. The board includes executives with industrial, financial, and pharmaceutical backgrounds. Notable independent directors include Carrie Cox (former pharmaceutical executive), Mark Blinn (former CEO of Flowserve), Todd Bluedorn (former CEO of Lennox International), and Janet Clark (former CFO of Marathon Oil). Their collective experience skews toward industrial and energy companies—a profile aligned with TI's customer base but not with semiconductor manufacturing or wireless technology at the system level.

The governance question the board faces is structural: it must evaluate a management team executing a decade-long capital program that will be judged in arrears. The 300mm manufacturing thesis will not be confirmed or refuted by the FCF/revenue line in any single year. Depreciation on Sherman and Lehi facilities will suppress margins through the late 2020s regardless of demand conditions. In that environment, the board's role is to hold management accountable to process—are capex commitments being made within the parameters of the framework, is utilization tracking toward the target trajectory, are synergy realization milestones being met—rather than to short-run financial outcomes. TI's compensation committee has historically tied long-run equity awards to TI-specific operational metrics rather than relative TSR to peers, which creates alignment with the long-duration thesis.
